summary: At a Sabbath meal in a leading Pharisee’s house, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, teaches about seats and guest lists, and tells the parable of the great supper.
key_insight: Jesus told His host to invite “the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind” (v. 13). In the parable, the master sends for exactly the same four (v. 21). God fills His own table with the guests He tells us to invite.
story: On a Sabbath Jesus went to eat in the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees, and they watched Him closely. In front of Him was a man with dropsy. Jesus asked the lawyers and Pharisees, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” They kept silent. So He took hold of the man, healed him and let him go. Then He asked, “Which of you, having a donkey or an ox that has fallen into a pit, will not immediately pull him out on the Sabbath day?” They had no answer.

Jesus noticed how the guests chose the best places, and He told them a parable. At a wedding feast, do not take the place of honor, in case someone more honored has been invited and the host says, “Give place to this man,” and you move in shame to the lowest place. Take the lowest place instead, so that the host may come and say, “Friend, go up higher.” “For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

Then He spoke to His host. When he gave a dinner, he should not invite his friends, brothers, relatives or rich neighbors, who would invite him back. “But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind. And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you; for you shall be repaid at the resurrection of the just.”

One of the guests said, “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God!” Jesus answered with a story. A man gave a great supper and invited many. At supper time he sent his servant to tell the guests, “Come, for all things are now ready.”

But they all began to make excuses. The first had bought a piece of ground and had to go and see it. Another had bought five yoke of oxen and was going to test them. Another said, “I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.”

The master of the house was angry. He told his servant, “Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the maimed and the lame and the blind.” The servant did so and reported, “Master, it is done as you commanded, and still there is room.” So the master sent him to the highways and hedges: “compel them to come in, that my house may be filled. For I say to you that none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper.”

scene.label: Dropsy
scene.text: Dropsy is swelling from fluid building up in the body, often a sign of serious illness of the heart, kidneys or liver. Luke says the man was simply there in front of Jesus. Whether the Pharisees placed him there as a test, Luke does not say, though they were watching closely.

scene.label: Places of honor
scene.text: At a formal meal, the places nearest the host carried the most honor, and guests were ranked by standing. Proverbs had already warned, “Do not exalt yourself in the presence of the king,” for it is better to be told, “Come up here” (Proverbs 25:6–7).

scene.label: Two invitations
scene.text: A host sent invitations ahead of time and then, when the meal was ready, sent servants to call the guests (compare Esther 6:14). To accept the first invitation and refuse the second was a public insult to the host.

scene.label: Thin excuses
scene.text: A man would hardly buy a field unseen or ten oxen untested, so both excuses are thin. A newly married man was excused from war for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5), not from a dinner. Each excuse sounds polite and means no.

scene.label: “Compel them”
scene.text: The word means to urge strongly. Poor strangers on the country roads would hardly believe a rich man’s invitation was meant for them. Centuries later Augustine used this line to justify forcing dissenters back into the church; in the story it describes the urgency of the invitation, not force.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke records this Sabbath meal, where Jesus turns a dinner party into a picture of the kingdom’s banquet. Matthew tells a similar parable of a king’s wedding feast in the temple during the last week (Matthew 22:1–14), with a different setting, different details and a harsher ending; many see two related parables told on different occasions. Luke’s version keeps at its center the people Jesus named in His first sermon at Nazareth: the poor, the brokenhearted, the captives and the blind (Luke 4:18).

seeing.reveals: Jesus heals in a house where He is being watched, then tells the guests, the host and the man who spoke of the kingdom what God’s table is really like. The invitation He carries is the master’s own: “Come, for all things are now ready.”
seeing.living: It is possible to say, “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God,” and still make excuses when the call comes. Answer the invitation now. Then set your own table for people who cannot pay you back.
seeing.ponder: What polite excuse have you been giving to Jesus’ invitation?

preaching.big_idea: God’s table is full of people who could never repay Him; only those who refused are missing.
preaching.watch_for: Four scenes share one table and one question: who gets a place? The guest’s pious remark (v. 15) sets up the parable; he assumes he will be at the kingdom’s feast, and Jesus answers with a story of invited guests who never came.
